title: Social Engineering & Payment Fraud
summary: Phone scams, fake support, tailgating and invoice fraud: the human side of hacking.

lessons.title: Hacking people, not computers
points: Social engineering manipulates people into giving access, information or money.
Common levers: authority ("I'm from head office"), urgency, helpfulness, fear, and curiosity.
It happens by phone, text, chat, social media and in person, not just email.

lessons.title: Business email compromise (BEC)
points: Criminals pose as a supplier or executive and ask to change bank details or make an urgent payment.
The FBI's 2024 Internet Crime Report recorded about $2.8 billion in BEC losses reported to it in a single year.
Defence: verify any payment or bank-detail change by calling a number you already have on file, never one in the request.
lessons.tip: A two-minute phone call can stop a six-figure loss.

lessons.title: Fake help desks & callers
points: Attackers call staff pretending to be IT, or call the help desk pretending to be staff, to reset passwords and MFA.
Caller ID can be spoofed. A familiar number or name doesn't prove who is calling.
Hang up and call back through the official number or ticketing system.

lessons.title: In the physical world
points: Tailgating: someone follows you through a secure door. Politely ask them to badge in or go to reception.
Lock your screen whenever you step away (Windows + L, or Ctrl + Cmd + Q on a Mac).
Don't plug in USB drives you find. Hand them to IT.

questions.q: A supplier emails saying their bank account has changed and asks you to pay this month's invoice to the new account. What should you do?
options: Reply to the email to confirm
Call the supplier on the number already on file to verify
Pay half to the old and half to the new account
questions.why: Bank-detail changes are the core of business email compromise. Verify through an independent, known contact, never details in the same message.

questions.q: If the caller ID shows your company's main number, the caller must be from your company.
questions.why: Caller ID is easy to spoof. Verify by hanging up and calling back through an official number.

questions.q: Someone carrying boxes asks you to hold the secure door open for them. What's the best response?
options: Hold the door, they look busy
Offer to help, but ask them to badge in or check in at reception
questions.why: Tailgating relies on politeness. You can be helpful and still make sure everyone uses their own access.

questions.q: Which psychological lever is used in: "This is the CFO. I need this transfer done in the next 30 minutes, don't tell anyone"?
questions.why: Claiming senior authority, adding a deadline and demanding secrecy are designed to bypass normal checks.

questions.q: Plugging in a USB stick you found in the car park to find its owner is a safe, helpful thing to do.
questions.why: Dropped USB devices are a known attack method and can run malicious code. Hand it to IT or security.

questions.q: A pop-up says your computer is infected and to call 'Microsoft Support' at a number shown. What is this?
questions.why: Real security warnings don't ask you to phone a number. Close the browser tab (or restart) and report it.

questions.q: What should you do when you leave your desk for a coffee?
options: Ask a colleague to watch it
questions.why: Locking takes a second (Windows + L) and stops anyone using your logged-in session.

email.subject: Updated remittance details – please action today
email.body:
Hello,

Due to an audit our banking has changed. Please use the attached new details for invoice #4471 and all future payments. We need payment today to avoid a late fee.

Kind regards,
Accounts Team

questions.why: A look-alike domain (supp1ies with a number 1), changed bank details and a same-day deadline. Call the supplier on the number you already have.

questions.q: Oversharing on social media (job role, manager's name, travel plans) can help attackers craft convincing scams.
questions.why: Attackers research targets online to make messages believable. Think about who can see what you post.

questions.q: A caller says they're from IT and need you to install a remote-access tool to fix an issue you didn't report. What do you do?
options: Hang up and contact IT through the official help desk
Ask them to email you the tool
questions.why: Unexpected support calls are a common way to get remote control of a computer. Verify through the official channel first.

questions.q: Verifying a request through a second, known channel is a good habit even when the request seems to come from your manager.
questions.why: Email accounts get hacked and voices can be cloned. Out-of-band verification is the most reliable defence.

sources.title: CISA – Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks
